text: Rosalba Carriera (12 January 1673 – 15 April 1757) was an Italian Rococo painter renowned for her pastel portraits, which helped popularize the medium in eighteenth-century Europe. She is remembered as one of the most successful women artists of any era. Born in Venice to Andrea Carriera, a lawyer, and Alba Foresti, an embroiderer and lacemaker, Carriera learned lace-making from her mother and engaged in crafts with her mother and sisters. The reasons for establishing her own studio are unknown, though early biographer Pierre-Jean Mariette suggested that when the lace industry declined, she needed a new source of income. The popularity of snuff-taking provided an opportunity, leading her to paint miniatures for snuff-box lids and as standalone works; she was among the first to use ivory instead of vellum as a support. By 1700, she was painting miniatures and completed her first pastel portraits in 1703. In 1704, she was made an Accademico di merito by the Roman Accademia di San Luca, a title for non-Roman painters. Between 1720 and 1721, she worked in Paris, where her work was in great demand; she was a guest of Pierre Crozat, painted Watteau, royalty, and nobility, and was elected a member of the Académie royale by acclamation. Her brother-in-law, Antonio Pellegrini, married to her sister Angela, was also in Paris and painted the ceiling of the Grande Salle in the Hotel de Nevers for John Law. Her sisters Giovanna and Angela accompanied her to France, with Giovanna helping her produce hundreds of portraits to support the family. Carriera’s Paris diary, published in 1793 by Antonio Zanetti (the Abbé Vianelli), and her extensive correspondence have been made available. Her work influenced the emerging aristocratic tastes in Paris, introducing a free style, vibrant color, and charm to the Rococo style, which soon dominated the arts. After returning to Venice in 1721, she visited Modena, Parma, and Vienna, where she was warmly received by rulers and courts. In 1730, she traveled to Vienna, where Emperor Charles VI became her benefactor, amassing over 150 of her pastels, and she in turn provided formal artistic training to the Empress; these works later formed the basis of the Alte Meister Gallery collection in Dresden. After Giovanna’s death in 1738, Carriera suffered deep depression and later lost her eyesight, possibly due to damage from painting miniatures in her youth; she underwent two unsuccessful cataract surgeries and eventually became completely blind. She outlived all her family and died at age 84 in a small house in the Dorsoduro district of Venice. Her mother taught her lace-making; her training as a portraitist is undocumented, though she may have studied with Antonio Lazzari, Federico Benecovich, Giuseppe Diamantini, and possibly copied Antonio Balestra’s work. There is speculation that Jean Steve encouraged her to paint miniatures on ivory for snuff-box lids, and she may have received oil technique instruction from Diamantini. She shared her skills with her sisters Giovanna and Angela and later taught female students such as Marianna Carlevarijs, Margherita Terzi, and Felicita Sartori. Carriera revolutionized pastel use by binding colored chalk into sticks, expanding the range and utility of the medium. Though criticized by Maurice Quai, a neoclassicist follower of Jacques-Louis David, as “The Rococo,” she played a key role in popularizing the style in France and England, where King George III acquired several of her works. Despite her prominence, she is often treated as an exception and overlooked, especially when Rococo fell out of fashion, a trend linked to gender bias; Sir Joshua Reynolds owned several of her pastels. Carriera was the first female painter to initiate a new style in the art community; the Rococo style emphasized pastel colors, spontaneous brushwork, dancing lights, subtle tonalities, and a soft, elegant approach. She was known for dragging the sides of white chalk across darker under-drawings to capture the shimmer of lace and satin, and for highlighting facial features and powdered hair. Her influence lasted nearly a century. She had many patrons, including Anton Maria Zanetti, who collected and promoted her works, and Joseph Smith, who also amassed a large collection; King George III purchased these works in 1762, including one of her self-portraits. Her best-known self-portrait is part of the Medici collection at the Uffizi Gallery in Florence, where she depicted herself with a brusque, honest appearance—featuring a larger nose, thin lips, and a deep dimple—holding a portrait of her sister and assistant Giovanna. Another self-portrait, Self-Portrait as an Old Woman (1746), shows mismatched eyes, reflecting her later eye problems. Carriera also created allegorical works such as ‘The Four Seasons,’ ‘The Four Elements,’ and ‘The Four Continents,’ featuring nymph-like women with symbolic elements. In September 2025, a Cambridge auction house sold a 1724 pastel portrait of Coulson Fellowes for £508,000, which had remained in a private collection since 1724 and was recorded in Carriera’s diary, executed during the sitter’s Grand Tour (1723–25). Carriera is best known for her innovative use of pastels, which had previously been used only for informal drawings, and for redefining pastel as a medium for serious portraiture that shaped the Rococo manner. She is a character in the novel The Laws of Time (2019) by Andrea Perego. Media related to her can be found at Wikimedia Commons.
